Checked against the Docker Hub API on 2026-08-17: bitnami/mongodb now describes itself as a Bitnami Secure Image and, over its first 400 tags, the only names that are not sha256-* digests are the rolling one and its metadata sibling. The free versioned images were moved to bitnamilegacy/mongodb, which is frozen at 8.0.13 from 2025-08-23. Replace both: mongo:8.0.29 (official, 315 MB) and nginx:1.30.4-alpine (official, 26 MB). Keep the two Countly images exactly as upstream names them, pinned: countly/api:25.03.52-LTS and countly/frontend:25.03.52-LTS, both published 2026-08-12."
20	  - "⛔⛔ YOUR ANALYTICS DATABASE LIVES ON THE APP VM AND NOTHING BACKS IT UP. redu has NO managed MongoDB, so unlike every Postgres entry in this library there is no separate database VM that survives the app. MongoDB runs as a container on the app VM with a named volume, which means: a named volume DOES survive re-uploading the source and running compose again on the same VM; it does NOT survive delete_deployment, a VM rebuild or the app VM being replaced, and there is no managed backup and no point-in-time restore. SAY THIS TO THE USER IN THOSE WORDS BEFORE THEY APPROVE THE PLAN. If the data matters, schedule a mongodump to somewhere off the VM as part of the handover; a dump you have never restored is not a backup."
21	  - "⛔ NGINX IS LOAD-BEARING AND ITS CONFIG IS NOT IN ANY IMAGE. redu proxies ONE port to ONE container, and Countly needs two: the SDK ingestion endpoints /i and /o are served by countly-api:3001 while the dashboard is countly-frontend:6001. Upstream's compose bind-mounts ./bin/docker/nginx.server.conf, so that file has to be in YOUR upload or nginx starts with the stock default and the dashboard 404s. Two deliberate changes from upstream, both explained there: the IPv6 listen line is dropped, and client_max_body_size is raised, because nginx defaults to 1 MB while api/config.sample.js allows a 200 MB upload, which makes large crash-symbol and image uploads fail with 413 while everything else looks perfect."

volumes:
  mongodb_data:

services:
  mongodb:
    image: mongo:8.0.29
    restart: unless-stopped

    command: ["mongod", "--bind_ip_all", "--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB", "2"]
    volumes:
      - mongodb_data:/data/db

    image: countly/api:25.03.52-LTS
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file:

    depends_on:

    env_file:

      # repo and signs the dashboard session cookie (app.js:644). Supplied through the project

      - COUNTLY_CONFIG_FRONTEND_WEB_SESSION_SECRET=[REDACTED:value]}
    depends_on:
      - mongodb

  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.30.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped

    volumes:
      - ./nginx.countly.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/countly.conf:ro

**Plan — Countly Community Edition on redu**

| | |
|---|---|
| Stack | `countly/api:25.03.52-LTS` + `countly/frontend:25.03.52-LTS` + `mongo:8.0.29` + `nginx:1.30.4-alpine`, one compose stack |

Files written and ready to upload: `docker-compose.yml`, `nginx.countly.conf`, `countly.env`, plus `redu-deploy-plan.md`.

Three things to read before you say go:

**Your analytics database lives on the app VM and nothing backs it up.** redu has no managed MongoDB, so unlike every Postgres app in this library there is no separate database VM that survives the app. Mongo runs as a container on the app VM with a named volume. That volume *does* survive re-uploading the source and running compose again on the same VM. It does *not* survive `delete_deployment`, a VM rebuild, or the app VM being replaced. There is no managed backup and no point-in-time restore. If the data matters, we schedule a `mongodump` off the VM on day one.

**m1.large is above the no-card trial ceiling** (m1.medium), so this needs a payment method on the account. Your quota fits it — 4 instances and 12 vCPUs free.

**The first visitor to `/setup` becomes the global admin**, and that window opens the moment the hostname answers. I'll claim the account myself as part of the deploy, before handing you the URL, then prove `/setup` returns 302 rather than 200. I need the email to claim it with.

  - "MEASURED 2026-08-17: THE API COMES UP LONG BEFORE THE FRONTEND, so /o/ping answering 200 does NOT mean the setup window is open yet. /o/ping went 200 at ~440s from deploy_compose returning, while /setup was still 502 and only started serving the form at ~540s (~9 minutes total).   - "SECURE COOKIES NEEDS TWO KEYS, NOT ONE. MEASURED 2026-08-17.   - "AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT THERE IS NO PUBLIC SIGNUP. Once a member exists, GET /setup redirects to /login and POST /setup returns User exists. Verified 2026-08-17 on the live instance: /i with an unknown app_key returns 400 {\"result\":\"App does not exist\"}, and /o/ping returns Success."
  - "DO NOT USE THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE AS WRITTEN.   - "THE OFFICIAL NGINX IMAGE PUTS THE CONFIG SOMEWHERE ELSE. Upstream bind-mounts its conf to /opt/bitnami/nginx/conf/server_blocks/countly.conf. On official nginx:alpine the path is /etc/nginx/conf.d/countly.conf. Mount it there or nginx starts on its stock default and the dashboard 404s."
  - "USE compose SERVICE NAMES, NOT CONTAINER NAMES, IN THE NGINX CONFIG. The redu VM runs docker and names the project app-src, so containers are app-src-countly-api-1.   - "YOUR ANALYTICS DATABASE LIVES ON THE APP VM AND NOTHING BACKS IT UP. redu has NO managed MongoDB.   - "NGINX IS LOAD-BEARING AND ITS CONFIG IS NOT IN ANY IMAGE. redu proxies ONE port to ONE container and Countly needs two: /i and /o are countly-api:3001, the dashboard is countly-frontend:6001.   - "PORT 8080, NOT 80. Upstream publishes 80:8080; this recipe publishes 8080:8080 and passes port 8080 to deploy_compose."
  - "SET COUNTLY_CONFIG_HOSTNAME TO THE FULL PUBLIC HOSTNAME. bin/docker/cmd.sh:5-7 errors when unset, on both containers. Generate the dname yourself in the full countly-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form and pass that exact string as dname; a bare label gets a random suffix appended."
  - "REPLACE THE SESSION SECRET, AND KEEP IT OUT OF THE REPO. config.sample.js ships web.session_secret as the literal countlyss. Pass COUNTLY_CONFIG_FRONTEND_WEB_SESSION_SECRET through deploy_compose's env (redu appends it to the project .env) and reference it in the compose file as ${COUNTLY_CONFIG_FRONTEND_WEB_SESSION_SECRET}, so the committed countly.env holds no credential.   - "passwordSecret IS A TRAP. api/config.sample.js has NO passwordSecret key, so per configextender an env override lands on passwordsecret, all lower case, which nothing reads, while the frontend applies the real one. Every member created afterwards would be locked out with a correct password. Confirmed 2026-08-17 that the deployed frontend resolves passwordSecret to \"\". LEAVE IT UNSET."
  - "THE ENV PREFIX DECIDES WHICH CONTAINER LISTENS, AND ONE SHARED ENV FILE IS SAFE. COUNTLY_CONFIG__<PATH> is applied by both, COUNTLY_CONFIG_API_<PATH> only by the api, COUNTLY_CONFIG_FRONTEND_<PATH> only by the frontend."
  - "DO NOT COPY THE QUOTES OUT OF THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE. It writes COUNTLY_CONFIG__FILESTORAGE=\"gridfs\" in a compose environment LIST, where the quotes become part of the value. Write plain unquoted values in your env file."
  - "FILE STORAGE IS GridFS. Uploaded images live IN MongoDB, so the Mongo volume is the single stateful thing on the VM. Set COUNTLY_CONFIG__FILESTORAGE=gridfs with the double underscore."
  - "USE restart: unless-stopped, NOT deploy.restart_policy. Upstream's compose is written for swarm and its deploy: block is ignored by docker compose, which would leave the stack dead after a VM reboot."
  - "AN env_file CHANGE NEEDS --force-recreate, NOT restart. docker compose restart reuses the old container environment. Use docker compose up -d --force-recreate <service> on the VM at /opt/app-src."
  - "MEASURED SIZING 2026-08-17, IDLE, FIRST BOOT: api 534 MiB, mongodb 256 MiB, frontend 196 MiB, nginx 5 MiB, about 1.0 GB of containers and 1.7 GB host used of 7.9 GB.   - "API WORKERS: image default 1, upstream compose 4. On m1.large (4 vCPU / 8 GB) beside MongoDB, COUNTLY_CONFIG_API_API_WORKERS=2 with --wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 2 ran fine at idle 2026-08-17."

# Self-host Countly on redu

Product and web analytics, crash reporting and push notifications, on infrastructure you own:
Countly Community Edition's own api and frontend images, a MongoDB container and a small nginx
router, on one VM with a public HTTPS URL.

About GBP 0.0486/hour, roughly GBP 35 a month. Above the no-card trial ceiling.

## Deploy log

- 2026-08-17: deployed successfully, deployment 448, m1.large, ~9 minutes from deploy_compose to a
  usable dashboard. Measured idle memory ~1.0 GB of containers on a 7.9 GB box. Two new quirks
  found and recorded: POST /setup is CSRF-protected, and secure cookies need
  COUNTLY_CONFIG_FRONTEND_COOKIE_SECURE as well as the WEB_SECURE_COOKIES key.
- 2026-08-17 deploy #448: ready, https://countly-ko6u7sxd.redu.cloud.

# Self-host Countly on redu

Product and web analytics, crash reporting and push notifications, on infrastructure you own:
Countly Community Edition's own api and frontend images, a MongoDB container and a small nginx
router, on one VM with a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Countly api and frontend** from their official pinned images, on one m1.large VM.
- **MongoDB 8.0** as a container on the same VM, with a named volume. redu has no managed MongoDB,
  so this is the whole database, and the section below is the part to read.
- **nginx** in front of both, routing the SDK ingestion paths to the api and everything else to
  the dashboard.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.0486/hour, roughly GBP 35 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Countly on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this before you approve: where your data lives

Every other database-backed entry in this library puts your data in a redu-managed database on its
own private VM, which outlives the app. **Countly cannot do that here, because redu has no managed
MongoDB.** Mongo runs as a container on the app VM, on a named volume.

What that means, precisely:

- The volume **survives** re-uploading your source and running compose again on the same VM.
- It does **not** survive `delete_deployment`, a VM rebuild, or the app VM being replaced.
- There is **no managed backup and no point-in-time restore**.

That is a real trade-off, not a footnote. If the analytics matter, schedule a `mongodump` to
somewhere off the VM on day one.

## The three that actually break it

**The first visitor owns it.** While no account exists, `/setup` hands the global-admin account
to whoever loads it. Nothing closes that window except claiming the account, so the recipe claims
it during the deploy and then proves `/setup` no longer answers 200. The claim is CSRF-protected:
GET first, carry the token and the cookie jar into the POST. Script below.

**The two Bitnami images.** The upstream compose pins neither to a version: `bitnami/mongodb` is
now a "Bitnami Secure Image" with no version tags left on the free repository, so there is nothing
to pin to. This recipe uses the official `mongo` and `nginx` images instead — which also moves the
nginx config mount to `/etc/nginx/conf.d/`.

**The nginx config.** It is bind-mounted from the repo rather than baked into an image, so it has
to travel in your upload. Without it the dashboard and the SDK endpoints cannot share one hostname.

## Claiming the admin account

Run this the moment `/setup` stops 502ing, before you hand the URL to anyone. It waits for the
form, then does the GET-then-POST that the CSRF filter requires. A bare POST gets
`403 Forbidden Token`, which is what this exists to avoid.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: HOST=countly-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud EMAIL=you@example.com bash claim-countly.sh
set -eu
HOST="${HOST:?set HOST}"
EMAIL="${EMAIL:?set EMAIL}"
PW="Cnt$(tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 20)!7Zq"   # digit + upper + symbol required

# 1. wait for the frontend, which comes up well after the api
for i in $(seq 1 150); do
  code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup" || echo 000)
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  [ "$code" = "302" ] && { echo "ALREADY CLAIMED: /setup redirects. Someone else may own this."; exit 1; }
  sleep 4
done

# 2. GET for the CSRF token, on a cookie jar the POST reuses
curl -sS -m 20 -c jar.txt -o setup.html "https://$HOST/setup"
CSRF=$(grep -oE '<input[^>]*name="_csrf"[^>]*>' setup.html \
       | grep -oE 'value="[^"]*"' | head -1 | sed 's/value="//;s/"$//')
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "no _csrf in the form"; exit 1; }

# 3. claim it
code=$(curl -sS -m 30 -b jar.txt -c jar.txt -o post.html -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "Referer: https://$HOST/setup" \
  --data-urlencode "_csrf=$CSRF" \
  --data-urlencode "full_name=Countly Admin" \
  --data-urlencode "username=admin" \
  --data-urlencode "email=$EMAIL" \
  --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "confirm_password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "lang=en" \
  "https://$HOST/setup")
[ "$code" = "302" ] || { echo "POST /setup -> $code"; head -c 300 post.html; exit 1; }
echo "claimed. username: admin"
echo "password: [REDACTED:value]"
```

## The check to run after the admin account exists

It proves it is talking to Countly before it asserts anything, and it treats "cannot tell" as its
own answer rather than as a pass.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: HOST=countly-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud bash check-countly.sh
set -u
HOST="${HOST:?set HOST to the public hostname}"
INCONCLUSIVE=3
TMP=$(mktemp -d)

# 1. POSITIVE: /o/ping proves nginx reached the api AND the api reached MongoDB.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o "$TMP/ping" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/o/ping" || echo 000)
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "000" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /o/ping answered $code. Still starting is the likely reason (upstream allows"
  echo "a 400 second health start period, and the first boot also loads city data). Re-run shortly."
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /o/ping answered $code, expected 200"; exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
if ! grep -q 'Success' "$TMP/ping"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /o/ping but not Countly's body:"; cat "$TMP/ping"
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
echo "OK  api container reachable through nginx, and it can read MongoDB"

# 2. POSITIVE: the dashboard is served through the SAME hostname.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -L -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -qi 'countly' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login answered $code and did not look like the dashboard"
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
echo "OK  dashboard served on the same hostname, so the nginx routing is right"

# 3. NEGATIVE, and it only means anything because 1 and 2 passed.
#    Polarity: a CLAIMED instance redirects /setup to /login. 200 is the failure.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup")
case "$code" in
  301|302)
    echo "PASS  /setup redirects, so a member exists and the admin seat is claimed"
    exit 0 ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL  /setup is still serving the first-admin form."
    echo "      Anyone who loads https://$HOST/setup right now becomes the global admin."
    echo "      Claim it immediately, or delete the deployment. Do not leave this running."
    exit 1 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup answered $code"; exit "$INCONCLUSIVE" ;;
esac
```

Countly Community Edition is AGPL-3.0 with a modified Section 7. Two things follow. Because you
operate the service over a network, AGPL Section 13 puts the source-offer obligation on you rather
than on redu. And the Section 7 addition forbids removing the Countly name, logo or links from any
interface an end user can see, so this is not something to white-label. Running an unmodified
instance for your own analytics is squarely inside both.

# Self-host Countly on redu

Product and web analytics, crash reporting and push notifications, on infrastructure you own:
Countly Community Edition's own api and frontend images, a MongoDB container and a small nginx
router, on one VM with a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Countly api and frontend** from their official pinned images, on one m1.large VM.
- **MongoDB 8.0** as a container on the same VM, with a named volume. redu has no managed MongoDB,
  so this is the whole database, and the section below is the part to read.
- **nginx** in front of both, routing the SDK ingestion paths to the api and everything else to
  the dashboard.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.0486/hour, roughly GBP 35 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Countly on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this before you approve: where your data lives

Every other database-backed entry in this library puts your data in a redu-managed database on its
own private VM, which outlives the app. **Countly cannot do that here, because redu has no managed
MongoDB.** Mongo runs as a container on the app VM, on a named volume.

What that means, precisely:

- The volume **survives** re-uploading your source and running compose again on the same VM.
- It does **not** survive `delete_deployment`, a VM rebuild, or the app VM being replaced.
- There is **no managed backup and no point-in-time restore**.

That is a real trade-off, not a footnote. If the analytics matter, schedule a `mongodump` to
somewhere off the VM on day one.

## The three that actually break it

**The first visitor owns it.** While no account exists, `/setup` hands the global-admin account
to whoever loads it. Nothing closes that window except claiming the account, so the recipe claims
it during the deploy and then proves `/setup` no longer answers 200. The claim is CSRF-protected:
GET first, carry the token and the cookie jar into the POST. Script below.

**The two Bitnami images.** The upstream compose pins neither to a version: `bitnami/mongodb` is
now a "Bitnami Secure Image" with no version tags left on the free repository, so there is nothing
to pin to. This recipe uses the official `mongo` and `nginx` images instead — which also moves the
nginx config mount to `/etc/nginx/conf.d/`.

**The nginx config.** It is bind-mounted from the repo rather than baked into an image, so it has
to travel in your upload. Without it the dashboard and the SDK endpoints cannot share one hostname.

## The nginx config to ship

Adapted from upstream's `bin/docker/nginx.server.conf`. Two deliberate changes, both marked:

```bash

server {
    listen 8080;
    # upstream also has: listen [::]:8080 ipv6only=on;
    # dropped, because a container without IPv6 in its netns makes nginx exit at start
    server_name _;

    # upstream sets no limit, so nginx's 1 MB default applies, while
    # api/config.sample.js allows a 200 MB upload. Raised to match.
    client_max_body_size 200m;
```

## Claiming the admin account

Run this the moment `/setup` stops 502ing, before you hand the URL to anyone. It waits for the
form, then does the GET-then-POST that the CSRF filter requires. A bare POST gets
`403 Forbidden Token`, which is what this exists to avoid.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: HOST=countly-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud EMAIL=you@example.com bash claim-countly.sh
set -eu
HOST="${HOST:?set HOST}"
EMAIL="${EMAIL:?set EMAIL}"
PW="Cnt$(tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 20)!7Zq"   # digit + upper + symbol required

# 1. wait for the frontend, which comes up well after the api
for i in $(seq 1 150); do
  code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup" || echo 000)
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  [ "$code" = "302" ] && { echo "ALREADY CLAIMED: /setup redirects. Someone else may own this."; exit 1; }
  sleep 4
done

# 2. GET for the CSRF token, on a cookie jar the POST reuses
curl -sS -m 20 -c jar.txt -o setup.html "https://$HOST/setup"
CSRF=$(grep -oE '<input[^>]*name="_csrf"[^>]*>' setup.html \
       | grep -oE 'value="[^"]*"' | head -1 | sed 's/value="//;s/"$//')
[ -n "$CSRF" ] || { echo "no _csrf in the form"; exit 1; }

# 3. claim it
code=$(curl -sS -m 30 -b jar.txt -c jar.txt -o post.html -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "Referer: https://$HOST/setup" \
  --data-urlencode "_csrf=$CSRF" \
  --data-urlencode "full_name=Countly Admin" \
  --data-urlencode "username=admin" \
  --data-urlencode "email=$EMAIL" \
  --data-urlencode "password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "confirm_password=[REDACTED:value]" \
  --data-urlencode "lang=en" \
  "https://$HOST/setup")
[ "$code" = "302" ] || { echo "POST /setup -> $code"; head -c 300 post.html; exit 1; }
echo "claimed. username: admin"
echo "password: [REDACTED:value]"
```

## The check to run after the admin account exists

It proves it is talking to Countly before it asserts anything, and it treats "cannot tell" as its
own answer rather than as a pass.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: HOST=countly-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud bash check-countly.sh
set -u
HOST="${HOST:?set HOST to the public hostname}"
INCONCLUSIVE=3
TMP=$(mktemp -d)

# 1. POSITIVE: /o/ping proves nginx reached the api AND the api reached MongoDB.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o "$TMP/ping" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/o/ping" || echo 000)
if [ "$code" = "502" ] || [ "$code" = "000" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /o/ping answered $code. Still starting is the likely reason (upstream allows"
  echo "a 400 second health start period, and the first boot also loads city data). Re-run shortly."
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /o/ping answered $code, expected 200"; exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
if ! grep -q 'Success' "$TMP/ping"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /o/ping but not Countly's body:"; cat "$TMP/ping"
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
echo "OK  api container reachable through nginx, and it can read MongoDB"

# 2. POSITIVE: the dashboard is served through the SAME hostname.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -L -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ] || ! grep -qi 'countly' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login answered $code and did not look like the dashboard"
  exit "$INCONCLUSIVE"
fi
echo "OK  dashboard served on the same hostname, so the nginx routing is right"

# 3. NEGATIVE, and it only means anything because 1 and 2 passed.
#    Polarity: a CLAIMED instance redirects /setup to /login. 200 is the failure.
code=$(curl -sS -m 20 -o "$TMP/setup" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/setup")
case "$code" in
  301|302)
    echo "PASS  /setup redirects, so a member exists and the admin seat is claimed"
    exit 0 ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL  /setup is still serving the first-admin form."
    echo "      Anyone who loads https://$HOST/setup right now becomes the global admin."
    echo "      Claim it immediately, or delete the deployment. Do not leave this running."
    exit 1 ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /setup answered $code"; exit "$INCONCLUSIVE" ;;
esac
```

Countly Community Edition is AGPL-3.0 with a modified Section 7. Two things follow. Because you
operate the service over a network, AGPL Section 13 puts the source-offer obligation on you rather
than on redu. And the Section 7 addition forbids removing the Countly name, logo or links from any
interface an end user can see, so this is not something to white-label. Running an unmodified
instance for your own analytics is squarely inside both.
